title: Is Brutal Honesty a Virtue or an Alibi?
script: Rangga: [thoughtful] You always frame your bluntness as integrity, Dinda, but I sometimes wonder whether it's really just cruelty that's found itself a respectable vocabulary.
Dinda: And you always frame your tact as kindness, Rangga, though half the time it looks to me like cowardice wearing a more presentable coat.
Rangga: [carefully] There's a difference between cowardice and consideration. I withheld my opinion of Bram's business plan because the timing would have crushed him unnecessarily.
Dinda: Or you withheld it because disagreeing felt uncomfortable, and you dressed that discomfort up afterward as concern for his feelings.
Rangga: [reflective] That's an ungenerous reading of a decision that, as far as I can tell, spared someone a devastating conversation he wasn't ready to have.
Dinda: Maybe. But he built three more months of momentum on a plan you privately considered doomed, and that cost him more than honesty would have.
Rangga: [honestly] I hadn't weighed it that way, admittedly. I suppose I measured the discomfort of the conversation rather than the cost of postponing it.
Dinda: Honesty isn't a bluntness contest, though, whatever you seem to assume about how I practice it. I choose my timing as carefully as you choose your silence.
Rangga: [gently] So where's the line between tact that protects someone and tact that simply protects you from an uncomfortable ten minutes?
Dinda: I ask myself whether my silence serves the other person or only my own comfort. If it's the latter, I've just repackaged cowardice.
Rangga: [calmly] By that measure, my silence with Bram served me more than it served him, however reasonable it felt at the time.
Dinda: That's a harder admission than most people manage.
Rangga: [encouraging] Don't get used to it. I still think you could deliver a hard truth with slightly more cushioning than you generally bother with.
Dinda: And I still think you could deliver an easy truth without waiting for the perfect, ever-elusive moment to arrive.
Rangga: [seriously] Perhaps we should each borrow a little from the other, then, before one of us does real damage with our preferred approach.
Dinda: Agreed. Starting with Bram, who deserves an honest conversation from at least one of us, sooner rather than later.

quiz.question: What does Rangga accuse Dinda of when it comes to her bluntness?
options: Being too diplomatic
Dressing up cruelty in a respectable vocabulary
Never sharing her real opinion
Only being honest with strangers
quiz.explanation: Rangga suggests her bluntness might really just be cruelty that has found a respectable vocabulary.

quiz.question: Why did Rangga withhold his real opinion of Bram's business plan?
options: He agreed with the plan completely
He believed the timing would have crushed Bram unnecessarily
He hadn't reviewed the plan yet
Bram never asked for his opinion
quiz.explanation: Rangga says he withheld his opinion because the timing would have crushed Bram unnecessarily.

quiz.question: What cost does Dinda point out from Rangga's silence?
options: Bram lost his job
Bram built three more months of momentum on a plan Rangga privately considered doomed
Bram found out from someone else immediately
There was no real cost
quiz.explanation: Dinda points out that Bram built three more months of momentum on a plan Rangga privately considered doomed.

quiz.question: How does Dinda test whether her own silence is justified?
options: She never questions her silence
She asks a third party to decide
She asks whether the silence serves the other person or only her own comfort
She assumes silence is always the safest choice
quiz.explanation: She asks herself whether her silence serves the other person or only her own comfort, calling the latter repackaged cowardice.

quiz.question: What do Rangga and Dinda agree to do by the end of the conversation?
options: Avoid Bram entirely
End their friendship over the disagreement
Each borrow a little from the other's approach, starting with an honest conversation with Bram
Let Bram figure things out alone
quiz.explanation: They agree to borrow from each other's approach and that Bram deserves an honest conversation from at least one of them soon.

quiz.question: What retrospective error does Rangga identify in sparing Bram discomfort?
options: He ignored the larger cost created by postponing necessary criticism.
Past sacrifice seemed to entitle him to greater control of the house.
Anger would consume energy without solving the shipment problem.
Later inconvenience cannot convert a commitment into an optional plan.
quiz.explanation: This interpretation follows the speaker's reasoning: He ignored the larger cost created by postponing necessary criticism.

quiz.question: How does Dinda reject the idea that honesty requires maximal bluntness?
options: Pride made both brothers wait indefinitely for the other's apology.
He delayed disclosure despite knowing the costs had changed.
Keeping a promise unwillingly differs from valuing the promise despite cost.
Truth can retain careful timing without being weakened.
quiz.explanation: This interpretation follows the speaker's reasoning: Truth can retain careful timing without being weakened.

quiz.question: Which diagnostic question separates tact from self-protection?
options: Ask whether silence serves the listener or the speaker's comfort.
His explanation sounds petty when translated into the family's present loss.
Reza must honour the price or absorb half the resulting loss.
She expects sufficient inconvenience to make most promises disappear.
quiz.explanation: This interpretation follows the speaker's reasoning: Ask whether silence serves the listener or the speaker's comfort.

quiz.question: Why does Rangga concede that his tact resembled cowardice?
options: Reconciliation does not require complete agreement about property.
A fair solution does not erase the supplier's poor handling.
Career inconvenience carries less weight than freely given commitment.
His silence protected him while Bram invested further in a failing plan.
quiz.explanation: This interpretation follows the speaker's reasoning: His silence protected him while Bram invested further in a failing plan.

quiz.question: What synthesis do both speakers accept at the end?
options: Honesty needs more care, while tact needs an earlier willingness to speak.
Restored brotherhood becomes more valuable than winning the original dispute.
Self-control shapes how objections are raised rather than eliminating them.
Commitment becomes morally meaningful when circumstances make it costly.
quiz.explanation: This interpretation follows the speaker's reasoning: Honesty needs more care, while tact needs an earlier willingness to speak.
